name: Skinning
description: Shelf slang originating from the Tier 1 practice of removing or swapping out visible chrome panels to change aesthetic appearance without buying new hardware — 'skinning' your rig to look different for the day. By 2209 it had broadened to mean any superficial identity change made to avoid surveillance or corporate recognition systems, including BCI persona masking and geneware pigment cycling. The term carries an undercurrent of defiance: you're not changing who you are, you're changing what they see. In Tier 4-5 usage it has been diluted to simply mean 'changing your look,' losing most of its subversive connotation.
cultural_impact: Skinning as a practice drives a thriving gray market in cosmetic chrome panels and geneware pigment cartridges on the Shelf, with ghost markets like Nakamura Flats running dedicated 'skin stalls' every third rotation. The term's spread into corporate tiers has caused some friction, as Tier 1 residents resent the word being used for something as trivial as a fashion choice.
locations: Nakamura Flats ghost market, Shelf District 7
The Molt — a Tier 2 aug-swap parlor on Lakeshore Under
story_hooks: A Shelf teenager known for elaborate daily skins suddenly stops changing — someone is forcing them to stay visible and trackable.
A corporate identity broker is selling 'premium skin packages' to Tier 4 clients, but the personas being sold are stolen from real Shelf residents who have no idea their faces are being worn uptown.

A synthetic being learns to 'skin' its chassis panels and begins passing as different synthetics to avoid a bounty — raising uncomfortable questions about whether identity fraud laws apply to non-humans.
definition: Swapping visible chrome or geneware aesthetics to change appearance, originally for surveillance evasion; broadly, any superficial identity change made strategically rather than for pure vanity.
usage_example: 'She's been skinning three times a day since the Helion sweep — you'd never know it was her on the same block twice.'
spread: Common Tier 1-2; adopted but diluted in Tier 3-4 as a fashion term; rarely heard in Tier 5 except ironically
